screens.title: Understanding XR Input Systems in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: Stepping into XR changes how you think about input. Instead of clicks and typed commands, users move, point, gaze, and reach in physical space. That means your app needs to translate position, orientation, button presses, and gestures into high-level interactions like select, grab, and teleport. Unity's XR Interaction Toolkit, or XRI, provides that bridge. It offers components and a workflow so you can declare what interactions should exist and then map those interactions to whatever hardware is present. In this chapter you’ll learn why abstracting input matters, how XRI’s Interactor and Interactable pattern reduces device-specific code, and the sequence to install the toolkit, enable an XR runtime, create an XR Origin, and wire up Input Action Assets. You’ll also practice a checklist to verify controllers are tracked and troubleshoot the common pitfall of unassigned input actions. By the end, you’ll understand not only the pieces but why this architecture makes XR projects more maintainable and cross-platform compatible. Think about one interactive object in your scene — by the end you should be able to make it respond to any controller without rewriting interaction logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Understanding XR Input
Understanding XR Input Systems in Unity
A practical walkthrough of XRI, XR Origin, and device-agnostic input.
In this lesson

You will learn the XRI pattern, install and enable plugin providers, create an XR Origin, and configure Input Action Assets so controllers register actions consistently.

Why it matters

Device-agnostic actions save time and let your scene respond the same way whether a user has an OpenXR headset or another runtime.

Explore Key Topics
XRI Pattern
Interactor and Interactable abstract interactions.
XR Origin
Root object for HMD and controllers.
Input Actions
Action Assets map logical actions to device inputs.
Concept Visual
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
2D Input
Mouse & keyboard. Pointer and clicks drive UI selection.
single-plane
3D XR Input
Gaze, tracked hands, and controllers provide position and orientation plus buttons and gestures.
spatial
XRI Role
XRI maps high-level interactions like select and grab to physical inputs across devices, so your scene logic stays device-agnostic.
Starter checklist
  • Install XR Interaction Toolkit from the Package Manager.
  • Enable an XR plugin provider like OpenXR in Project Settings.
  • Create an XR Origin and assign Input Action Assets to controllers.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to think in spatial interactions rather than mouse clicks, set up Unity's XR Interaction Toolkit, and wire action-based controllers to a playable XR Origin. First, you will learn to differentiate 2D input patterns from 3D XR input paradigms, recognizing what changes when a user can move and reach in space. Second, you will explain the role of the XR Interaction Toolkit and why abstracting interactions saves time across devices. Third, you will identify common XR devices and configure their capabilities through an Input Action Asset so the same logical action fires on different hardware. Finally, you will create an XR Origin and connect left and right XR Controller components to Input Action Assets so grab and select actions work. Each objective includes a practical milestone you can verify in the Editor, like checking that a controller's select action triggers an Interactable. These skills matter because they reduce platform-specific code and help your scene behave correctly whether you test with OpenXR or another provider.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map directly to actions you can take in the Editor. You will install the XR Interaction Toolkit from the Package Manager and accept recommended defaults so Unity creates the XR Interaction Manager and suggested settings. You will enable an XR plugin provider like OpenXR in Project Settings, which prepares the runtime for HMDs and controllers. You will create an XR Origin GameObject and inspect its camera offset, main camera, and child controller GameObjects. For each controller you will find the XR Controller (Action-based) component and assign an Input Action Asset that defines actions such as Select, Activate, and Grab. The practical outcome is that when a user presses a mapped button, the Interactor raises an event that an Interactable can respond to. If something fails to register, you will use a small checklist — verify the XR Interaction Manager has the Default Input Actions set, confirm action maps are enabled, and ensure the XR Origin is active. These steps make sure your scene is ready for testing with a physical headset.

Install & enable XRI
Open Package Manager, install XR Interaction Toolkit, and accept recommended samples and settings.
Enable XR Plugin Provider
Enable OpenXR or your target provider in Project Settings to allow runtime tracking.

screens.title: 2D vs 3D Input Paradigms
screens.narratorSegment: When you design for screens, input centers on a single plane: the display. A mouse or finger maps a 2D position to a UI element and a click or tap triggers an action. In XR, input lives in three dimensions. The user’s head and hands carry position and orientation, which means interactions depend on reach, pointing direction, and continuous spatial data rather than a one-off cursor. This changes both sensing and UX. For example, selecting an object can be done by a ray from a controller or by directly touching it with a virtual hand. A concrete example: grabbing a mug in VR requires detecting a close-range overlap, mapping a grab action to a button or a hand-closing gesture, and then applying physics or attachment logic. A common misconception is that you can reuse mouse-driven UI logic unchanged; you cannot, because spatial inputs require attention to distance, occlusion, and 6-degree-of-freedom orientation. To adapt, think in terms of Interactors (tools that probe space) and Interactables (objects that define what happens when probed). As a takeaway, design your interactions around affordances in space — reachable surfaces, collision volumes, and natural gestures — rather than screen coordinates. Try asking: does this interaction rely on orientation, distance, or a discrete button press?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › 2D vs 3D Input
2D Input (Mouse / Touch)
  • Single plane coordinates and discrete clicks or taps.
  • UI focused; hover and focus states originate from cursor position.
  • Interaction is often instantaneous and local to the viewport.
Concrete example
Clicking a button to open a menu uses a 2D coordinate and a discrete input event.
3D XR Input (HMD, Controllers, Hands)
  • Position and orientation matter; interactions depend on reach and direction.
  • Continuous tracking enables gestures, rays, and direct manipulation.
  • Mapping buttons to logical actions must respect spatial context.
Misconception
Treating XR as 2D UI will break affordances like grabbing and occlusion.
Tip
Use distance thresholds for direct grabs to avoid accidental picks.
Takeaway
Model interactions as spatial affordances, not clicks.
Check your understanding
How would you detect a grab versus a point select in space?

screens.title: What is the XR Interaction Toolkit (XRI)?
screens.narratorSegment: The XR Interaction Toolkit is Unity’s high-level framework for building interactive XR experiences. Its core idea is to separate interaction intent from device specifics: you declare logical actions like select, activate, or grab, and XRI connects those to physical inputs through controllers and input actions. This reduces duplicated code because you don’t write a separate handler for each controller type. A concrete example: instead of checking the trigger button name on many controllers, you configure a Select action in an Input Action Asset and bind it to the trigger on the left and right XRController. Interactors are the tools users wield — a ray interactor projects a pointing beam, a direct interactor detects overlap for hand touches. Interactables are components placed on scene objects that define how they respond, such as XRGrabInteractable for pick-up behavior or XRSocketInteractor for placement. A common misconception is that XRI removes the need to think about device nuance; in reality, you still test device behavior, but XRI centralizes mapping and interaction logic so testing and maintenance are easier. The key takeaway is that XRI gives you a predictable, reusable interaction model across platforms.

keyIdea.title: XRI purpose
keyIdea.text: Provide a reusable, component-driven API so you declare interactions once and map them to multiple devices.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › XR Interaction Toolkit
XRI — definition and role
A high-level toolkit that connects logical actions to physical inputs across XR devices through components like Interactors and Interactables.
Interactors
Tools on the controller or gaze origin that initiate interactions, such as rays or direct overlap spheres.
Interactables
Components on objects that define responses: grab, hover, select, or socket behavior.
Analogy
Think of Interactors as tools like a virtual hand or pointer, and Interactables as objects that have rules for how those tools affect them.
Common mistake
Assuming XRI auto-maps all devices without assigning or enabling the correct Input Action Assets; always verify mappings and action map activation.

screens.title: Interactors and Interactables — The Interaction Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: At the heart of XRI is a simple contract: Interactors probe, Interactables respond. Interactors live on controller or gaze GameObjects; they detect potential targets using rays, overlap checks, or proximity. Interactables live on scene objects and implement behaviors for hover, select, activate, and attach. For example, an XR Ray Interactor will cast a ray and report potential targets to the XR Interaction Manager. When the user performs a Select action — mapped through an Input Action Asset — the Interactor issues a select event. An XRGrabInteractable listens for that event and attaches the object to the Interactor’s attach transform, optionally enabling physics. A concrete scenario: you create a toolbox item with XRGrabInteractable and a controller with XR Direct Interactor; when hands overlap and the user presses the mapped grab button, the object becomes attached. A common misconception is that Interactors must be identical for all hands; you can use different Interactor types for different contexts, for instance a ray for distant pointing and a direct interactor for close manipulation. The core takeaway is to design Interactors to represent the user’s tool and Interactables to encapsulate how objects should behave when touched, pointed at, or grabbed.

keyIdea.title: Interaction contract
keyIdea.text: Interactor detects and requests actions; Interactable defines how the object reacts, enabling clear separation of concerns.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Interactors & Interactables
Interactor (tool)
Examples: XR Ray Interactor, XR Direct Interactor. Responsible for detecting targets and raising interaction events.
Key behaviors
  • Detect targets (raycast or overlap)
  • Raise hover/select/activate events
  • Attach or manipulate objects when appropriate
Interactable (object)
Examples: XRGrabInteractable, XRSimpleInteractable. Defines how an object responds to events raised by any Interactor.
Grab behavior
Attach to the Interactor, optionally transfer physics ownership.
Socket behavior
Define a slot that accepts objects when released.
Scenario
A ray interactor selects a distant button, while a direct interactor picks up a nearby tool; both use the same Interactable scripts so object behavior is consistent.

screens.title: Common Interactor Types
screens.narratorSegment: XRI provides several Interactor types suited for different interaction patterns. The XR Ray Interactor projects a ray from a controller or hand and is ideal for distant selection, UI pointing, and precision placement. A common concrete use case is pressing a floating menu button across the room: the ray finds the button collider, hover events fire, and then the Select action triggers the interaction. The XR Direct Interactor detects collisions or proximity for near-field interactions and is the right fit for picking up objects by reaching and touching them. Gaze or head-based Interactors can be used where users rely on head orientation to point; this is common in simple AR experiences or seated VR where hands may be unavailable. A frequent misconception is to use a ray for everything; doing so can make manipulation feel unnatural for close objects because you lose the intuitive hand-to-object contact. Choose Interactor types to match the intended affordance: ray for distance, direct for touch, and gaze when hands are not the primary tool. Finally, remember that different Interactors can coexist so one hand might use a direct interactor while the other uses a ray.

keyIdea.text: Select an Interactor type that matches distance and affordance: ray for distant pointing, direct for near manipulation, gaze for head-based input.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Common Interactor Types
XR Ray Interactor
Projected ray for distant selection and UI pointing. Use when precision at range matters.
XR Direct Interactor
Proximity-based interactor for touching and grabbing nearby objects with natural contact.
Gaze / Head Interactor
Uses head orientation for selection; useful in limited-input scenarios or AR gaze UX.
Example
A toolbox demo uses a direct interactor for grabbing tools and a ray interactor for toggling distant switches; both interactor types raise the same logical events consumed by Interactables.

screens.title: Interactable Types and Behaviors
screens.narratorSegment: Interactables are how scene objects describe their response to interactions. The XRGrabInteractable is a common Interactable that enables physics-aware grabs and attachments; when selected, it typically attaches to the Interactor’s attach transform and may disable gravity or change rigidbody kinematic state. XRSocketInteractor defines a receptacle; when an object is released near the socket, it snaps into place. XRSimpleInteractable is useful for objects that respond to select or activate without full grab semantics, such as buttons or levers. A concrete example: make a toy car grab-able with XRGrabInteractable so users can pick it up, drive it around, and place it into a XRSocketInteractor garage to lock it into position. A common pitfall is forgetting to set colliders or attach points; without a proper attach transform, objects can rotate or offset unexpectedly when grabbed. The best practice is to provide a clearly placed attach transform and tune physics settings for natural movement. The takeaway is to choose the Interactable that matches the desired behavior and to test attachments and release logic on real hardware when possible. Interactable Types and Behaviors means select xrgrabinteractable for full pick-up behavior, xrsocketinteractor for placement, and xrsimpleinteractable for buttons and lightweight actions.. In practical terms, grabables, sockets, and simple interactables explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Interactable Types
XRGrabInteractable
Enables picking up and holding objects, with attach transforms and physics options.
XRSocketInteractor
Defines slots that accept compatible Interactables and snap them into a defined pose.
XRSimpleInteractable
Lightweight responses for buttons, toggles, or activations without full grab semantics.
Practical tip
Always provide a small attach transform and test release behavior; misaligned attaches cause visual jumps during grabs.

screens.title: Install XRI and Enable an XR Plugin Provider
screens.narratorSegment: The first practical steps are installing the XR Interaction Toolkit and enabling an XR plugin provider. Start by opening the Package Manager, choose Unity Registry, search for XR Interaction Toolkit, and install it. Unity often prompts to import recommended samples and apply default interaction settings — accept those defaults to create helpful starter GameObjects like the XR Interaction Manager. Next, open Project Settings and select XR Plugin Management; under the Plugins tab enable the provider you plan to target, for example OpenXR. Enabling a provider configures the runtime for HMD and controller tracking. A concrete reason for this sequence is that XRI expects an active runtime to surface device inputs; without a plugin provider, controllers won’t be tracked even if XRI is installed. A common troubleshooting step when tracking fails is to restart Unity after enabling the plugin and then ensure the XR Interaction Manager exists in the scene. The takeaway: installation and plugin enablement are separate but necessary actions — both must succeed before controller inputs will surface in Play Mode. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Install & Enable
Step-by-step
  1. Open Window → Package Manager and select Unity Registry.
  2. Search and install XR Interaction Toolkit, accept recommended defaults.
  3. Open Edit → Project Settings → XR Plugin Management.
  4. Enable OpenXR or your target provider and apply settings.
Why order matters
XRI installation provides components; enabling a plugin provider activates runtime tracking required for controllers to report input in Play Mode.
Troubleshoot
If controllers aren’t tracked, verify the XR Interaction Manager exists, the Default Input Actions are assigned, and restart Unity after enabling plugins.

screens.title: Create an XR Origin and Inspect Components
screens.narratorSegment: The XR Origin is the root that represents the user's physical presence in the scene. Create one by right-clicking the Hierarchy and choosing XR → XR Origin (VR/AR). The created GameObject typically contains a Camera Offset, the Main Camera, and child GameObjects for the LeftHand Controller and RightHand Controller. Inspect the left and right controller children: each should have an XR Controller (Action-based) component if you selected the action-based template. The XR Origin also often places an XR Interaction Manager in the scene automatically. The camera represents the HMD, so moving the HMD moves the camera relative to the XR Origin’s transform. A practical test is to enter Play Mode with a connected headset and watch the Main Camera update in real time; if the controllers are not represented, verify the controllers have the XR Controller (Action-based) component and that their Input Action Asset is correctly assigned. A common misconception is that XR Origin is required only for VR; it’s also the central structure for AR scenes where camera and input sources must be coordinated. The key takeaway is to confirm your XR Origin contains appropriate controller children with action-based components before wiring inputs.

screens.title: Input Action Assets and Action Maps
screens.narratorSegment: Input Action Assets are Unity assets that group logical actions into action maps and allow multiple device bindings per action. An action map might be named XR Controller and contain actions such as Select, Activate, and Grab. Each action can have multiple bindings; for example, Select can be bound to the left trigger and the right trigger so either controller triggers the same logical action. This abstraction is crucial because it lets Interactors subscribe to an action rather than a device-specific input. A concrete illustration is the simplified JSON representation of an Input Action Asset: it shows the Select action with bindings for LeftHand triggerPressed and RightHand triggerPressed, and the Activate action bound to gripPressed on both hands. A common misconception is to edit these assets only by hand — Unity provides a graphical editor that makes configuring action maps and bindings safer. The core takeaway is to ensure your action maps have all necessary logical actions and that each XR Controller component references the Input Action Asset so event propagation works correctly at runtime. Input Action Assets and Action Maps means define logical actions and bind multiple device inputs so interactors can raise consistent events across hardware.. In practical terms, how actions like select and activate are represented and bound. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Input Action Assets
Structure
Action maps group actions. Actions define semantics. Bindings map actions to device paths and interactions.
Editor
Use the Input Action Asset editor to add action maps, actions, and bindings. Duplicate the XRI Default Input Actions to customize for your project.
Example binding (visual)
{
  "name": "XR Controller",
  "actions": [
    { "name": "Select", "type": "Button", "bindings": [
        { "path": "<XRController>{LeftHand}/triggerPressed", "interactions": "Press" },
        { "path": "<XRController>{RightHand}/triggerPressed", "interactions": "Press" }
    ]},
    { "name": "Activate", "type": "Button", "bindings": [
        { "path": "<XRController>{LeftHand}/gripPressed", "interactions": "Press" },
        { "path": "<XRController>{RightHand}/gripPressed", "interactions": "Press" }
    ]}
  ]
}
Tip
Ensure the XR Controller (Action-based) component on each controller references the same Input Action Asset so actions are available to Interactors.

screens.title: Assigning Input Action Assets to Controllers
screens.narratorSegment: Once you have an Input Action Asset configured, assign it to your XR Controller (Action-based) components. In the Hierarchy, expand XR Origin → Camera Offset → LeftHand Controller and RightHand Controller. Select each controller and find the XR Controller (Action-based) component. Set the Input Action Asset field to your customized XRI Default Input Actions. This makes the controller publish Select, Activate, and other actions. Next ensure the XR Interaction Manager in the scene has its Default Input Actions field assigned to the same asset; this lets the manager enable action maps and route actions to Interactors. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Assign Actions
Steps to assign
  1. Expand XR Origin and select LeftHand Controller.
  2. In XR Controller (Action-based), set Input Action Asset to your asset.
  3. Repeat for RightHand Controller.
  4. Select XR Interaction Manager and set Default Input Actions to the same asset.
Validation

Common pitfall
Controllers are tracked but actions don’t fire because the action asset is not assigned to the controller or the interaction manager.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: A handful of recurring issues cause controllers or actions to appear nonfunctional. First, the XR Interaction Toolkit might be installed but the XR Plugin Provider is not enabled; that results in no runtime tracking. Second, the XR Origin might be missing or inactive; without an XR Origin your Main Camera and controllers aren’t tied to the expected root. Third, Input Action Assets may not be assigned to the XR Controller (Action-based) components or the XR Interaction Manager; actions must be referenced so the system can enable their maps. For example, developers sometimes duplicate the default asset but forget to assign the duplicate, so the scene still points at the original. Another common problem is disabling action maps in script without re-enabling them at runtime, leaving no active bindings. A concrete troubleshooting flow: verify XR Plugin Management has a provider enabled, confirm XR Origin exists and is active, check that LeftHand and RightHand controllers reference an Input Action Asset, and open the XR Interaction Manager to validate Default Input Actions. If tracking still fails, restart Unity and rebuild if needed. The key takeaway: methodically check installation, provider enablement, XR Origin presence, and action asset assignments to resolve most issues.

Quick checklist
  • Is XR Interaction Toolkit installed and updated?
  • Is an XR Plugin Provider enabled in Project Settings?

If controllers track but actions do not fire, open the XR Interaction Manager and confirm the Default Input Actions field references your Input Action Asset. Assign it if empty and restart Play Mode.
Pro tip
Keep a single canonical Input Action Asset for the project and reference it everywhere to avoid mismatches between duplicated assets.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the core concepts to keep in mind. First, the XR Interaction Toolkit provides a high-level A P I to make interactions device-agnostic. Second, an Interactor represents the user's tool — a ray, direct hand, or gaze origin — and it raises hover and select events. Third, an Interactable encapsulates how an object responds to those events, enabling grabs, sockets, and simple activations. Remember these three definitions and how they map to real objects in your scene. When you design interactions, ask which tool a user will use and how the object should behave when probed. These ideas reduce duplicated code and make interactions predictable across headsets and controllers. As you continue, keep testing on real hardware and verify that your Input Action Assets, XR Origin, and Interactor types fit the affordances you intend to support.

fullNarratorScript:
Stepping into XR changes how you think about input. Instead of clicks and typed commands, users move, point, gaze, and reach in physical space. That means your app needs to translate position, orientation, button presses, and gestures into high-level interactions like select, grab, and teleport. Unity's XR Interaction Toolkit, or XRI, provides that bridge. It offers components and a workflow so you can declare what interactions should exist and then map those interactions to whatever hardware is present. In this chapter you’ll learn why abstracting input matters, how XRI’s Interactor and Interactable pattern reduces device-specific code, and the sequence to install the toolkit, enable an XR runtime, create an XR Origin, and wire up Input Action Assets. You’ll also practice a checklist to verify controllers are tracked and troubleshoot the common pitfall of unassigned input actions. By the end, you’ll understand not only the pieces but why this architecture makes XR projects more maintainable and cross-platform compatible. Think about one interactive object in your scene — by the end you should be able to make it respond to any controller without rewriting interaction logic.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to think in spatial interactions rather than mouse clicks, set up Unity's XR Interaction Toolkit, and wire action-based controllers to a playable XR Origin. First, you will learn to differentiate 2D input patterns from 3D XR input paradigms, recognizing what changes when a user can move and reach in space. Second, you will explain the role of the XR Interaction Toolkit and why abstracting interactions saves time across devices. Third, you will identify common XR devices and configure their capabilities through an Input Action Asset so the same logical action fires on different hardware. Finally, you will create an XR Origin and connect left and right XR Controller components to Input Action Assets so grab and select actions work. Each objective includes a practical milestone you can verify in the Editor, like checking that a controller's select action triggers an Interactable. These skills matter because they reduce platform-specific code and help your scene behave correctly whether you test with OpenXR or another provider.

These objectives map directly to actions you can take in the Editor. You will install the XR Interaction Toolkit from the Package Manager and accept recommended defaults so Unity creates the XR Interaction Manager and suggested settings. You will enable an XR plugin provider like OpenXR in Project Settings, which prepares the runtime for HMDs and controllers. You will create an XR Origin GameObject and inspect its camera offset, main camera, and child controller GameObjects. For each controller you will find the XR Controller (Action-based) component and assign an Input Action Asset that defines actions such as Select, Activate, and Grab. The practical outcome is that when a user presses a mapped button, the Interactor raises an event that an Interactable can respond to. If something fails to register, you will use a small checklist — verify the XR Interaction Manager has the Default Input Actions set, confirm action maps are enabled, and ensure the XR Origin is active. These steps make sure your scene is ready for testing with a physical headset.

When you design for screens, input centers on a single plane: the display. A mouse or finger maps a 2D position to a UI element and a click or tap triggers an action. In XR, input lives in three dimensions. The user’s head and hands carry position and orientation, which means interactions depend on reach, pointing direction, and continuous spatial data rather than a one-off cursor. This changes both sensing and UX. For example, selecting an object can be done by a ray from a controller or by directly touching it with a virtual hand. A concrete example: grabbing a mug in VR requires detecting a close-range overlap, mapping a grab action to a button or a hand-closing gesture, and then applying physics or attachment logic. A common misconception is that you can reuse mouse-driven UI logic unchanged; you cannot, because spatial inputs require attention to distance, occlusion, and 6-degree-of-freedom orientation. To adapt, think in terms of Interactors (tools that probe space) and Interactables (objects that define what happens when probed). As a takeaway, design your interactions around affordances in space — reachable surfaces, collision volumes, and natural gestures — rather than screen coordinates. Try asking: does this interaction rely on orientation, distance, or a discrete button press?

The XR Interaction Toolkit is Unity’s high-level framework for building interactive XR experiences. Its core idea is to separate interaction intent from device specifics: you declare logical actions like select, activate, or grab, and XRI connects those to physical inputs through controllers and input actions. This reduces duplicated code because you don’t write a separate handler for each controller type. A concrete example: instead of checking the trigger button name on many controllers, you configure a Select action in an Input Action Asset and bind it to the trigger on the left and right XRController. Interactors are the tools users wield — a ray interactor projects a pointing beam, a direct interactor detects overlap for hand touches. Interactables are components placed on scene objects that define how they respond, such as XRGrabInteractable for pick-up behavior or XRSocketInteractor for placement. A common misconception is that XRI removes the need to think about device nuance; in reality, you still test device behavior, but XRI centralizes mapping and interaction logic so testing and maintenance are easier. The key takeaway is that XRI gives you a predictable, reusable interaction model across platforms.

At the heart of XRI is a simple contract: Interactors probe, Interactables respond. Interactors live on controller or gaze GameObjects; they detect potential targets using rays, overlap checks, or proximity. Interactables live on scene objects and implement behaviors for hover, select, activate, and attach. For example, an XR Ray Interactor will cast a ray and report potential targets to the XR Interaction Manager. When the user performs a Select action — mapped through an Input Action Asset — the Interactor issues a select event. An XRGrabInteractable listens for that event and attaches the object to the Interactor’s attach transform, optionally enabling physics. A concrete scenario: you create a toolbox item with XRGrabInteractable and a controller with XR Direct Interactor; when hands overlap and the user presses the mapped grab button, the object becomes attached. A common misconception is that Interactors must be identical for all hands; you can use different Interactor types for different contexts, for instance a ray for distant pointing and a direct interactor for close manipulation. The core takeaway is to design Interactors to represent the user’s tool and Interactables to encapsulate how objects should behave when touched, pointed at, or grabbed.

XRI provides several Interactor types suited for different interaction patterns. The XR Ray Interactor projects a ray from a controller or hand and is ideal for distant selection, UI pointing, and precision placement. A common concrete use case is pressing a floating menu button across the room: the ray finds the button collider, hover events fire, and then the Select action triggers the interaction. The XR Direct Interactor detects collisions or proximity for near-field interactions and is the right fit for picking up objects by reaching and touching them. Gaze or head-based Interactors can be used where users rely on head orientation to point; this is common in simple AR experiences or seated VR where hands may be unavailable. A frequent misconception is to use a ray for everything; doing so can make manipulation feel unnatural for close objects because you lose the intuitive hand-to-object contact. Choose Interactor types to match the intended affordance: ray for distance, direct for touch, and gaze when hands are not the primary tool. Finally, remember that different Interactors can coexist so one hand might use a direct interactor while the other uses a ray.

Interactables are how scene objects describe their response to interactions. The XRGrabInteractable is a common Interactable that enables physics-aware grabs and attachments; when selected, it typically attaches to the Interactor’s attach transform and may disable gravity or change rigidbody kinematic state. XRSocketInteractor defines a receptacle; when an object is released near the socket, it snaps into place. XRSimpleInteractable is useful for objects that respond to select or activate without full grab semantics, such as buttons or levers. A concrete example: make a toy car grab-able with XRGrabInteractable so users can pick it up, drive it around, and place it into a XRSocketInteractor garage to lock it into position. A common pitfall is forgetting to set colliders or attach points; without a proper attach transform, objects can rotate or offset unexpectedly when grabbed. The best practice is to provide a clearly placed attach transform and tune physics settings for natural movement. The takeaway is to choose the Interactable that matches the desired behavior and to test attachments and release logic on real hardware when possible. Interactable Types and Behaviors means select xrgrabinteractable for full pick-up behavior, xrsocketinteractor for placement, and xrsimpleinteractable for buttons and lightweight actions.. In practical terms, grabables, sockets, and simple interactables explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The first practical steps are installing the XR Interaction Toolkit and enabling an XR plugin provider. Start by opening the Package Manager, choose Unity Registry, search for XR Interaction Toolkit, and install it. Unity often prompts to import recommended samples and apply default interaction settings — accept those defaults to create helpful starter GameObjects like the XR Interaction Manager. Next, open Project Settings and select XR Plugin Management; under the Plugins tab enable the provider you plan to target, for example OpenXR. Enabling a provider configures the runtime for HMD and controller tracking. A concrete reason for this sequence is that XRI expects an active runtime to surface device inputs; without a plugin provider, controllers won’t be tracked even if XRI is installed. A common troubleshooting step when tracking fails is to restart Unity after enabling the plugin and then ensure the XR Interaction Manager exists in the scene. The takeaway: installation and plugin enablement are separate but necessary actions — both must succeed before controller inputs will surface in Play Mode. Install XRI and Enable an XR Plugin Provider means install xr interaction toolkit via package manager and enable an xr plugin provider like openxr in project settings before testing controllers.. In practical terms, steps to prepare your unity project for xr input. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The XR Origin is the root that represents the user's physical presence in the scene. Create one by right-clicking the Hierarchy and choosing XR → XR Origin (VR/AR). The created GameObject typically contains a Camera Offset, the Main Camera, and child GameObjects for the LeftHand Controller and RightHand Controller. Inspect the left and right controller children: each should have an XR Controller (Action-based) component if you selected the action-based template. The XR Origin also often places an XR Interaction Manager in the scene automatically. The camera represents the HMD, so moving the HMD moves the camera relative to the XR Origin’s transform. A practical test is to enter Play Mode with a connected headset and watch the Main Camera update in real time; if the controllers are not represented, verify the controllers have the XR Controller (Action-based) component and that their Input Action Asset is correctly assigned. A common misconception is that XR Origin is required only for VR; it’s also the central structure for AR scenes where camera and input sources must be coordinated. The key takeaway is to confirm your XR Origin contains appropriate controller children with action-based components before wiring inputs.

Input Action Assets are Unity assets that group logical actions into action maps and allow multiple device bindings per action. An action map might be named XR Controller and contain actions such as Select, Activate, and Grab. Each action can have multiple bindings; for example, Select can be bound to the left trigger and the right trigger so either controller triggers the same logical action. This abstraction is crucial because it lets Interactors subscribe to an action rather than a device-specific input. A common misconception is to edit these assets only by hand — Unity provides a graphical editor that makes configuring action maps and bindings safer. The core takeaway is to ensure your action maps have all necessary logical actions and that each XR Controller component references the Input Action Asset so event propagation works correctly at runtime. A handful of recurring issues cause controllers or actions to appear nonfunctional. First, the XR Interaction Toolkit might be installed but the XR Plugin Provider is not enabled; that results in no runtime tracking. Second, the XR Origin might be missing or inactive; without an XR Origin your Main Camera and controllers aren’t tied to the expected root. Third, Input Action Assets may not be assigned to the XR Controller (Action-based) components or the XR Interaction Manager; actions must be referenced so the system can enable their maps. For example, developers sometimes duplicate the default asset but forget to assign the duplicate, so the scene still points at the original. Another common problem is disabling action maps in script without re-enabling them at runtime, leaving no active bindings. A concrete troubleshooting flow: verify XR Plugin Management has a provider enabled, confirm XR Origin exists and is active, check that LeftHand and RightHand controllers reference an Input Action Asset, and open the XR Interaction Manager to validate Default Input Actions. If tracking still fails, restart Unity and rebuild if needed. The key takeaway: methodically check installation, provider enablement, XR Origin presence, and action asset assignments to resolve most issues.

Here are the core concepts to keep in mind. First, the XR Interaction Toolkit provides a high-level A P I to make interactions device-agnostic. Second, an Interactor represents the user's tool — a ray, direct hand, or gaze origin — and it raises hover and select events. Third, an Interactable encapsulates how an object responds to those events, enabling grabs, sockets, and simple activations.
